IV10-01.note: Clean. Wary = on one's guard; no second reading. Distractors are all affect/manner words that a student who half-knows the word could reach for (curious = also alert, polite = also restrained), so each is wrong for a locatable reason. Key word 'guarded' is slightly harder than the prompt, which is fine at this level. Explanation matches the final options exactly.

IV10-02.note: Deft is a staple ISEE word; I would call this easy rather than medium. The three distractors are all approving character terms, so they model the student who knows deft is complimentary but not what it compliments - exactly the right failure mode. Explanation's axis ('none says how well it is done') is accurate against the final set.

IV10-03.note: Easy, not medium - lethargic is high-frequency. 'Forgetful' is the working distractor (lethargic misread as mentally dull); 'anxious' catches the student who remembers only that the word names a bad state. Explanation consistent with final options.

IV10-04.note: Key is right and unarguable. But the distractor set is the thinnest in the synonym half: costly, formal, recent share no axis with rudimentary, so a student who does not know the word is guessing at random rather than being tempted. 'Recent' has a faint hook (rudiment = beginning, so 'just started'), 'formal' none at all. Not a defect that drops the item; the weakest of the 14.

IV10-05.note: 'Escort' is the good one - goad's cattle-driving origin makes 'drive/lead along' a real wrong path, and it is wrong for a reason. 'Praise' catches goad-as-encouragement. Exclusive: provoke is the only option that carries pressure. Explanation matches final options.

IV10-06.note: 'Weary' is doing real work as the insolent/indolent confusion trap, though 'idle' would have been the sharper form of it (and is used as a distractor in IV10-11). 'Evasive' models the student who knows insolent is about how you treat someone but not that it affronts. Exclusive - evasive dodges, it does not disrespect. Explanation matches.

IV10-07.note: Medium rather than hard; quandary appears on most ISEE Upper lists. The distractors are correctly all situation-nouns (good category discipline) but none is semantically attractive: only 'delay' has a hook (quandary confused with quagmire/stuck). A student who does not know the word gains nothing from elimination. Key is exclusive and the explanation tracks the final set.

IV10-08.note: All four options share the 'adj + to + verb' frame, so form gives nothing away - good. 'Slow to anger' is the genuine trap (resilient misread as unflappable/hard to upset), which is a mistake real students make. Explanation matches the final phrasing of all four.

IV10-09.note: Correctly hard. 'Harmless' and 'costly' both trade on rife's negative collocations (rife with corruption/disease), so they catch the student who has the connotation but not the sense; 'brief' is the weakest of the three. Exclusive. Explanation's 'a thing can be any of those and still be confined to one corner' is exactly the discriminating axis and matches the final options.

IV10-10.note: Well built: all four are privations, so the parallel is tight and only the object of the want separates them (the explanation's 'want of company / strength / clarity' framing is the right one and is accurate against the final set). 'Solitude' picks up the penury/penitence-monastic association. Exclusive.

IV10-11.note: Hardest synonym here, because the KEY is itself a hard word - a student can know churlish and still be unsure of surly. That is legitimate at Upper Level but means this item tests two words, worth knowing when placing it. 'Idle' is a strong distractor via churl = peasant/lout. Exclusive; none of timid/boastful/idle entails unpleasantness toward others. Explanation matches.

IV10-12.note: 'Postpone' is the direction-reversal trap and is the right kind of wrong - same axis (pace), opposite sign - and the explanation says so in those terms. 'Approve' catches expedite-as-process-paperwork. Exclusive.

IV10-13.note: Best-constructed synonym set in the batch: sponsor, rival, witness, judge are four roles in one dispute, so the category cannot be used to eliminate and the student must know which role arbitrates. Medium rather than hard (arbiter is common). Explanation's 'all four turn up in a dispute, but only one decides it' is accurate to the final options.

IV10-14.note: Uniform 'adverb + participle' frame across all four - no formal tell. 'Rarely seen' is the useful distractor for the student who knows palpable turns up in 'a palpable silence' and guesses at 'uncanny/rare'. Exclusive. Explanation matches final wording.

IV10-15.note: Every distractor is fur-appropriate (tangled, trimmed, faded), so the option set cannot be filtered by topic - good design for an easy item. 'Tangled' is the near miss but the sentence supplies rain, not matting, and 'completely soaked' is what an afternoon of hard rain entails. Exclusive. Explanation matches the final stem.

IV10-16.note: Key is right and exclusive. Two rationale-vs-stem frictions, neither fatal, both worth recording: (a) the explanation rebuts 'overgrown' with 'would need months rather than the days Ito was away', but the final stem never states a duration - it says only that he left Thursday and she returned; the inference is sound but the explanation asserts a fact the stem does not carry; (b) the explanation rebuts 'scorched' with 'would need direct sun', while the final stem does place the ferns on a windowsill, which implies sun. Scorched is still wrong - the causal chain the sentence builds is the missed watering - but the rationale rebuts it on the one ground the stem partly concedes. Recommend rewording both rebuttals to lean on the unwatering rather than on time and sun.

IV10-17.note: 'Strategy' is a genuinely strong distractor because 'where to stand' and 'when to pass' can be read as tactical, and a hurried student will stop there. It is still not defensible: 'every player was new to the sport' plus 'the first three practices' fixes the list as first principles. Exclusive. Colon-list construction gives the reasoning without giving the word.

IV10-18.note: Key exclusive and well cued - the stem is entirely about duration (different family each spring, not two years running), so 'permanent' is forced. The distractors are the weak point: costly/profitable inject money the sentence never raises and 'confusing' attaches to the wrong noun, so none models a real misreading of the stem. Closest to a real hook is 'profitable' (a student imagining the rule blocks families from working a plot for gain). Item is sound; the set does not earn its four options.

IV10-19.note: 'Provisional' is the best distractor - it is the right register and also explains why riders distrust the sign, but it makes a claim about the sign's original intent that the stem does not support. 'Unofficial' catches the student who reasons from 'riders check their phones instead'. Exclusive: only 'outdated' is entailed by 'not changed since the route moved'. Explanation matches final stem and options.

IV10-20.note: 'Impatient' is the strongest single distractor in the sentence-completion half - the situation (same four questions all day, stopped listening) invites it, and only 'though still accurate' plus the absence of any reported feeling rules it out. That is a distractor wrong for a reason a real student falls for, which is what this batch wants. Exclusive. Explanation rebuts all three on the final wording.

IV10-21.note: Closest call among the items I still voted exclusive. 'Precaution' reads naturally in the frame ('not an accident but a precaution') and someone could tell a story where staff prop the door deliberately for egress. What decides it is the evidence the stem actually supplies: the discriminating fact is repetition - the same wedge on all six visits - and repetition supports habituality, not purpose; nothing in the stem gestures at a safety motive, and 'the violation' frames it as wrongdoing. Misunderstanding and coincidence are pre-excluded by 'not an accident', so effectively this is a two-option item. Explanation matches the final stem.

IV10-22.note: 'narrow but -------' demands a positive contrast, which kills fragile immediately and recent nearly so; 'local' is the designed trap and is flatly refuted by the four-hour drive, so a student who skims the first clause lands on it. Exclusive. Explanation's arithmetic ('eight hours on the road') is correct against the final stem's 'four hours each way'.

IV10-23.note: Medium rather than hard: 'Although' plus 'choked with old snow' determines blank one before the options are read, and only one pair survives. 'difficult . . . plan' is the right trap for a student who ignores the concessive. Both halves of the key are ordinary words, which is what keeps this from being hard. Exclusive; explanation tracks the final stem.

IV10-24.note: All four options are antonym pairs in the same 'yet' frame, so pair-shape gives nothing away and the student must map the colon's two illustrations onto the two blanks. Vocabulary (austere/lavish, impersonal/intimate) is properly Upper Level. I would call the reasoning medium because the colon supplies both halves explicitly. Exclusive. Explanation accurate against the final options.

IV10-25.note: Correctly hard and the key is the only option that reconciles 'ran higher' with 'the weather had not changed'. One logical soft spot for the record, which does not make a second option defensible: strictly, moving the gauge two miles east changes the place being measured, so higher totals could mean the new site is wetter rather than that the old figures were low - the stem forecloses the temporal confound but not the spatial one. Every alternative option is still worse, so exclusivity holds. 'Rounded' is the best distractor (the explanation's rebuttal - rounding goes both ways - is the correct one).

IV10-26.note: 'Habitual' is a real rival and the second-closest call in the batch: 'across the whole hour' supplies consistency, which is habit's evidence, and 'came to look, on reflection' signals the same kind of deflating revision. It loses because the stem's one concrete detail is that the failure story converts a failure into a credit - that is craft, and habit does not explain construction. 'Sincere' is the naive first read the sentence is built to overturn. Exclusive, but the margin here is the thinnest of the items I passed; if any item in this batch draws a split with another grader, expect it to be this one. Explanation matches the final stem.

IV10-27.note: Hard rather than medium - not for the reasoning, which is clean, but because 'flattering' applied to a NUMBER (an optimistic estimate) is a figurative extension many strong 13-year-olds will not have met. 'Cautious' is the good distractor: it is the right register and the right axis and merely points the wrong way, which is the mistake a student makes when they know the figure is unreliable but not in which direction. 'Exact' is pre-killed by the warning clause. Exclusive; explanation matches.

IV10-28.note: Key right and exclusive, but this is the easiest sentence completion in the batch and is marked medium. The phrase 'in words' does nearly all the work by collocation alone: perform/recall/doubt all sit badly with it before any meaning is considered, so a student can answer without engaging the contrast the sentence sets up (knowing a test by ear vs stating it). The item would be harder and the distractors would earn their place if the rival options were themselves verbs of articulation. Explanation is accurate to the final stem, including the 'though every one of them knew it' clause it leans on twice.

IV10-29.note: Correctly hard, and hard for the right reason: the student must infer an intention from three release choices rather than decode a word. Misquoted/contested/celebrated all presuppose engagement, which every detail in the stem is designed to prevent, so the elimination is clean and the key is exclusive. Slight register note - 'ignored' is the more idiomatic completion, but 'unread' is precise and is the only option consistent with 'calculated to leave it'. Explanation matches the final stem.

IV10-30.note: THE ONE ITEM I WOULD DROP. 'Luck' is defensible and the stem actively supports it. The defense: the sentence says the shop HAPPENS TO SIT on the one corner where three bus lines meet - 'happens to' is an explicit marker of fortune, not of design, so an owner who 'puts this down entirely to luck, since the shop happens to sit on the one corner where three bus lines meet' is saying something fully coherent and idiomatic. The surrounding frame reinforces it: the shop sells out daily and has NEVER ADVERTISED, so the owner is portrayed as declining credit for anything he did, and attributing a windfall to luck is precisely that gesture. 'Location' and 'luck' are also not parallel options - the corner IS the location, and luck is the explanation of why he has it, so a student who reads the since-clause as naming the cause picks location and one who reads it as naming the accident picks luck, and both are reading the same words correctly. The explanation compounds this rather than resolving it: its entire rebuttal of luck is 'mere chance - the sentence points at a specific piece of ground instead', which never addresses 'happens to', the one word in the stem that makes luck live. Fix is cheap and does not touch the key: delete 'happens to' ('since the shop sits on the one corner where three bus lines meet'), or replace the 'luck' option with a non-overlapping noun such as 'habit'. Flagged separately as the one place where a final-stem word contradicts its own rationale.
